newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran conservatives criticise Khatami cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Iran conservatives criticise Khatami cabinet.

text.p: Conservative members of Iran's parliament on Tuesday sharply criticised several of President Mohammad Khatami's cabinet nominees on the first day of debates vetting the candidates.
All 22 minister designates must receive a vote of confidence from the conservative-led parliament, or Majlis, to take office.

"Some deputies and newspapers reason that since President Khatami received 20 million votes in the election, we have to vote for all the ministers. But the Majlis has 24 million votes behind it," said deputy Abufazel Razavi Ardakani.

He was apparently answering comments by pro-Khatami deputies who had voiced thinly veiled warnings to conservatives that it was politically unwise to vote against ministers proposed by a president who enjoyed wide support.
Khatami, who was elected president in May by a landslide from among a 33-million electorate, earlier on Tuesday asked the 270-seat parliament to approve all of his cabinet choices.
More than 15 deputies earlier backed the moderate Shi'ite Moslem cleric's cabinet choices during an initial five-hours set aside for delegates urging support for a vote of confidence.
But conservative deputies lashed out at some of the nominees during the day's second round of debate set aside for critics.

Razavi Ardakani accused culture minister designate Ataollah Mohajerani -- controversial for his 1990 support for direct talks with Washington and his moderate views -- of being too "culturally tolerant and politically weak vis-a-vis the West".
Deputy Mehdi Reza Darvishzadeh also singled out Mohajerani for having contacts with liberal and opposition intellectuals.
"Can someone who helps deviant political tendencies ... fight a cultural invasion as a minister?", Darvishzadeh said.
Deputy Ahmad Nejabat said: "The main danger at this sensitive time is cultural leniency and liberalism and we promise ... to resist it to the last drop of our blood."

The Culture and Islamic Guidance Ministry has emerged as a battleground between Khatami's backers, who want to breathe more freedoms into the Islamic republic, and conservatives who see the organisation as a key weapon against a "Western cultural invasion".
The ministry decides what media, books, films and music are allowed in the country.
Razavi Ardakani also criticised interior ministry designate Abdollah Nouri, casting doubt on his loyalty to the assembly and the country's supreme spiritual leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
"His track record shows he attaches no value to the Majlis. He isn't 100 percent obedient to the leadership," he said of Nouri, who ran the interior ministry from 1989 to 1993.
Oil minister designate Bijan Namdar Zanganeh also came under fire from Razavi Ardakani, who accused him of mismanagement during the last nine years as energy minister.

Parliamentarian Davoud Danesh Jafari blasted agriculture ministry nominee Issa Kalantari, retained in his post by Khatami, accusing him of corruption and blaming him for Iran's increased dependence on imports of wheat and other foodstuffs.

On a more conciliatory note, influential conservative deputy Mohammad Reza Bahonar said: "Despite our principled criticism, we respect Mr Khatami's choices and will give our vote of confidence to most of the ministers, except for two or three."
Khatami, 54, was swept to power by the votes of youth, women and the middle class who saw him as a leader able to increase social and economic freedom.
The parliament was scheduled to vote on Wednesday after a third five-hour session during which the cabinet nominees would defend themselves and their programmes.
Pro-Khatami MPs earlier on Tuesday threw their support behind Mohajerani and the other minister designates.
Several deputies reminded parliament that Mohajerani had quickly withdrawn his proposal for Iran-U.S. talks and commended him as an experienced administrator and cultural authority.
